summary: This local news photo essay examines the barriers people with disabilities still face on public transit more than three decades after the ADA, through accounts of broken elevators, crumbling sidewalks, outdated information and malfunctioning bus lifts. It contrasts these problems with NewCal City, whose "Universal Design" approach, audit, training center, wayfinding tools, new fleet and community engagement show what inclusive transit can look like. The piece argues for moving beyond mere compliance toward genuine accessibility.
one_line: A photo essay on persistent ADA transit barriers contrasted with NewCal City's Universal Design overhaul of its accessible public transportation system.
key_facts: About 61 million Americans have disabilities and often face obstacles using public transportation.
The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was signed into law on July 26, 1990, as landmark civil rights legislation including equal access to public transportation.
On October 14, 2023, Elizabeth Thompson found a broken elevator at the downtown transit hub.
John Mansfield, a visually impaired commuter, faces danger from crumbling sidewalks and poorly marked crosswalks as city budgets tighten and maintenance backlogs grow.
On September 25, 2023, Sarah Keller could not find the accessible subway entrance because the transit authority's website information was outdated.
Bus driver Mike Rodriguez had to turn away a passenger because the bus's wheelchair lift malfunctioned, a problem tied to aging transit fleets.
NewCal City introduced an approach called "Universal Design" on November 1, 2023, aiming to go beyond mere compliance toward inclusivity.
NewCal City's initiative broke ground on December 5, 2023, starting with an extensive audit of its transit system to identify barriers.
The Marian Tetley Center for Accessible Transit opened on March 10, 2024, and is named after a local disability rights advocate.
The Marian Tetley Center houses a mock-up transit station with simulated vehicles for rider learning and transit staff sensitivity and operational training.
NewCal City added a mobile app with real-time updates and tactile maps at stations to help riders with visual and cognitive disabilities.
NewCal City's new buses and trains accommodate mobility devices and have adjustable seating and improved communication systems for riders with sensory disabilities.
NewCal City held town hall meetings, public forums and user experience workshops so people with disabilities could shape the changes.
The transit authority partnered with local businesses, disability rights organizations and technology firms, yielding financial support, software development and educational programs.
